daf7c6ca1a:
This is the architect-level view of splitting work across Claude agents. It covers:

  • why one context stops being enough;
  • what the split costs in tokens, latency and failure probability;
  • how to choose a topology and a decomposition axis;
  • how to write the contract between agents;
  • how to design for partial failure and for trust boundaries;
  • how to prove with an ablation that the split earned its bill.

CCAR-F chapters 2 and 4 teach the mechanics (the Task tool, briefs, fan-out). This chapter is the decision layer above them. Exam weights and domain names come from third-party blueprint summaries; verify them against the official exam guide.
bdc48fc4f2: Reading time: 3 to 3.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 17 runnable Python examples plus 2 Java files: ccarp-companion/03-multi-agent-decomposition/. Run bash run_all.sh; every Python example works offline with --mock.
b52724d270:
A multi-agent system trades tokens, latency variance and coordination risk for three things a single agent cannot give you: contexts that stay small and focused, work that runs in parallel, and permission boundaries between the parts of a task.

So the architect's job is to prove, with numbers from the requirements card and a measured ablation, that at least one of those three is worth its price for this workload, and then to cut the work along the axis where the pieces need each other least.
88dd576e45:
Everything else in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

  • The cost model exists because the trade is real and checkable before you build anything.
  • The latency model exists because parallelism changes a sum into a maximum, and a maximum over many noisy workers has a tail.
  • The decomposition axes exist because a bad cut produces duplicated work, holes, and subagents that need information somebody else holds.
  • The task contract exists because subagents start with nothing, and the lead has to be able to reject their answers mechanically.
  • The trust-boundary section exists because, in an enterprise, the most defensible reason to split an agent is often not speed at all.
  • The failure model, the state table, the governance controls and the evaluation design exist because a system of ten workers fails in ways a system of one does not.

CCAR-P is the exam that asks whether you noticed.
6a58329082:
Read the exam through the lens of the blueprint. Domain 1 asks you to select patterns (workflow, augmented LLM, agent, multi-agent) against a requirements card. The cheapest pattern that meets the card wins.

The questions are rarely "how do you spawn a subagent". They look more like this: here is a workload with a latency target, a volume, a budget and a data-sensitivity constraint; which design, and what do you measure before you commit? The right answer usually refuses the more elaborate design, or accepts it for a stated reason with a stated number.

The distractors are the designs that sound scalable: a hierarchy of agents "for flexibility", a peer swarm "for resilience", one agent per field of a form.
96edfbb535:
Three habits will carry you through almost every question in this chapter.

  1. State the requirement as a number before choosing a design (p95 latency, cost per task, per-class accuracy, coverage).
  2. Ask what the extra agents buy that a better prompt, a better tool or a workflow would not.
  3. Look for the governance consequence: who can write, who can read untrusted text, who approves, where the trace lives.

The chapter has two running examples: a carrier network-operations centre investigating regional degradations, and a retailer auditing supplier contracts. Both have the properties that make multi-agent designs tempting: breadth, long evidence trails, expensive humans. And both have constraints that make them dangerous: SLAs, per-class thresholds, regulated data.
8e4b7937b7: Splitting a hard problem among cooperating workers is older than language models. Every failure mode in this chapter was discovered before. Knowing the lineage tells you which old lessons apply, and which new properties (non-determinism, natural-language interfaces, token cost) are genuinely different.
700ac504b4:
The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system at Carnegie Mellon (mid to late 1970s) introduced the blackboard architecture. Independent knowledge sources, each expert in one level of the problem (acoustics, syllables, words, syntax), read from and write to a shared data structure. They cooperate opportunistically, with no central plan.

Around the same time, Carl Hewitt's actor model described computation as independent actors that communicate only by asynchronous messages.

Both ideas survive today in the "peer / shared state" topology. Both also left a lesson that modern LLM swarms rediscover. With no owner of termination and no ownership of the shared state, the system is flexible, hard to bound, and hard to audit.
0c2e91d81f:
Reid Smith's Contract Net protocol (1980) framed distributed problem solving as a market. A manager announces a task. Contractors bid. The manager awards the task to the best bid and receives the result.

Three ideas in that description are directly useful now. A task has an explicit specification. The contractor reports a result the manager can evaluate. And the manager stays accountable for the whole. The modern "task contract" in section 10 is the same idea, with a prompt where the announcement used to be.
b45ac7ebcd:
Domain-driven design (Evans, 2003) gave architects the rule for cutting systems. Split along bounded contexts, where each part has its own model and a narrow, explicit interface, and keep chatty interactions inside one context. That is the rule for cutting agent work too.

The enterprise-integration literature then separated orchestration (one party drives the flow) from choreography (parties react to each other's events). Every Spring architect who has debugged a choreographed saga knows why regulated systems lean towards orchestration.

MapReduce (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) made the fan-out and fan-in pattern routine. Its practical lesson was about stragglers. The job finishes when the slowest task finishes, so the framework launches backup copies of the last tasks. Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" (2013) generalised that into the arithmetic you will use in section 06. When a request fans out to many workers, the tail of the slowest worker dominates user-visible latency.
3145c2c56d:
Once models could call tools, frameworks appeared that let several model-backed agents converse: AutoGen from Microsoft Research (2023), CrewAI, LangGraph and others. The early demonstrations were chat-style, with a planner, a coder and a critic exchanging messages. They were impressive, and they were expensive. Many failed in production for the old reasons: no owner of termination, no budget, no audit trail.

Anthropic's December 2024 essay "Building effective agents" drew the distinction this chapter relies on. On one side are workflows, where code orchestrates the model calls through predefined paths. On the other are agents, where the model directs its own process. The essay recommended finding the simplest solution first, and adding complexity only when it measurably helps.

It also named patterns, among them prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation and orchestrator-workers. In that last one, a central model breaks a task down dynamically and delegates to workers. Check the essay for the exact wording.
bf9309dd37:
In June 2025 Anthropic published an engineering write-up of its multi-agent Research feature. Its numbers frame the economics architects need. It reported three things:

  • agents typically used about 4 times the tokens of a chat interaction, and multi-agent systems about 15 times;
  • token usage explained most of the variance in performance on its browsing evaluation;
  • a lead on a larger model with subagents on a smaller one outperformed a single larger-model agent by about 90 percent on its internal research evaluation.

Check the source for the exact figures and conditions.

The same write-up said where multi-agent designs fit: breadth-first work with many independent directions, information that exceeds one context window, and many complex tools. They fit poorly when agents must share a lot of context or have many dependencies. The write-up said that describes most coding tasks.

A widely read counter-argument came from another agent-product team, also in mid-2025 (find it by searching for "don't build multi-agents"). It made the same point from the other side. When sub-agents act on partial views of the same context, they make conflicting decisions. So share context, and keep a single thread for tightly coupled work.

Meanwhile, Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK shipped subagents as a first-class feature, with their own context, tools and model.
643775b029: The two positions do not conflict. They are the two halves of the same decision rule, and the exam tests whether you can tell which half your scenario sits in. On one side: breadth, volume of evidence and trust boundaries. On the other: coupling, shared state and low value per task.
23b4fa10d7: A single agent works inside one context window, and four properties of that arrangement limit it. Each limit is a reason to split only if it is binding for your workload. So each comes with the measurement that tells you whether it is.
634bfb463f:
Everything the agent reads stays in the window for the rest of the run, and it is re-read on every call. In the NOC example, each site contributes about 2,400 tokens of tool results (active alarms plus a bulky history). After 20 sites the window holds about 68,000 tokens. Perhaps 3,000 of them matter for the site being analysed now.

Two things follow. The first is cost. Input tokens over a run grow with the square of the number of calls, because call k re-reads everything from calls 1 to k-1 (CCAR-F chapter 1, section 7).

The second is quality. Models tend to attend less reliably to the relevant fact as irrelevant material accumulates around it. How much quality is lost depends on the task and the model, so do not assert a threshold. Measure it: run your evaluation set at several context sizes and plot accuracy against tokens in context.

A subagent that sees one site never has that problem. Its window holds about 6,400 tokens at the start, and perhaps 15,000 after five exploration turns.
9c8185b147:
Consider an agent that must handle alarms, KPIs, configuration, ticketing, billing look-ups and credit issuance. It carries all of those tool definitions on every call and pays for them in tokens. And it chooses among them with a precision that falls as the list grows. Chapter 6 treats capability bloat directly.

The multi-agent angle is that splitting by capability gives each agent a short, coherent tool list. The sharper point is permissions. One agent holding both "read customer e-mail" and "issue credit" gives a single prompt-injection a path to a financial action. Splitting by privilege puts a boundary between them that the model cannot talk its way across (section 12).
5513b72752:
A single agent processes independent items one after another. If one site takes 30 seconds of model and tool time, 20 sites take about 10 minutes at the median, and a 30-site incident takes 16 minutes. Say the NOC's target is a root-cause hypothesis in under 15 minutes. Then serial processing fails the SLA before quality is even considered.

Parallelism turns the sum into a maximum plus overhead (section 06). This is the clearest case where a number on the requirements card justifies multi-agent.
28b8f6a96e:
Picture a system prompt that must make the agent expert in RF engineering, billing disputes and contract law. It is long, internally conflicting, and impossible to evaluate piece by piece. Separate agents have separate prompts that can be versioned, tested and changed independently. That is a lifecycle argument (chapter 16) as much as a technical one.

It also gives you separate failure domains. A malformed answer from the transport specialist does not corrupt the RAN specialist's context.
c5b4407fb6:
None of these limits is a reason to split on its own authority. A workflow with a parallel step and a single model call per branch gets the latency win without autonomous subagents. A well-designed tool that returns 200 tokens instead of 2,400 removes most of Limit 1.

Splitting by agent is the right answer only when two things hold. The branches need to decide what to do next, because their path depends on what they find. And the other fixes are not enough. That condition, branches that need their own agentic loop, separates "orchestrator-workers" from "parallelisation" in the Anthropic taxonomy. It is also what separates a subagent from a function call.
acb4f00f19: CCAR-F chapters 2 and 4 cover how to spawn a subagent and how to write its brief. At architect level, think of a subagent as four independent levers you set, each with a cost and a risk. The design question is which levers you need.
e35aae36a3: A fifth thing is not a lever but a consequence: the interface between lead and subagents. In a microservice estate you would write an API contract and a consumer-driven test. Here the interface is a natural-language brief going out and a JSON object coming back. It deserves the same discipline (section 10).
66f2c53603:
The first number an architect should produce for any multi-agent proposal is the token bill. Stakeholders will ask about it, and it is the number most often guessed. The model needs only a few measured quantities:

  • B, the base context every call carries (system prompt, tool definitions, task);
  • R, the tokens one unit of work adds to the context as tool results;
  • o, the output tokens per turn;
  • N, the number of independent units (sites, contracts, stores).

For the NOC example the companion code uses B = 6,000, R = 2,400, o = 350, and a 350-token summary returned by each subagent. These are assumptions. Replace them with numbers from a trace of your own system (chapter 10).
0e2b08b58c:
The single agent. It handles each unit in a tool turn and a reasoning turn, so it makes about 2N + 1 calls. Call k re-sends the base plus everything accumulated so far. So the input tokens over the whole run are roughly (2N+1)·B + (R+2o)·N².

The N² term is the whole story: doubling the breadth roughly quadruples the input bill. The peak context is B + N(R+2o), and that is where the quality limit (section 03) bites.
60a6d149cf:
The orchestrator. Each subagent pays for its own base, the contract, and a short loop of its own. With T exploration turns its input is about T·(B + contract) + R·T(T-1)/2. That is a constant per unit, so the total is linear in N.

The lead pays twice: once to plan and write contracts, once to synthesise. Its second call carries N summaries. The lead's context grows by only about 350 tokens per unit.

The constant per unit decides everything, and its main driver is T, how many turns a cold-started subagent needs. A subagent cannot use what the lead or its siblings already know, so it explores from scratch.
46e5ebfa22: Running it with the default assumptions gives the table below. The defaults are five exploration turns per subagent, plus placeholder prices for a stronger lead tier and a cheaper worker tier. Read the last two columns: the ratios of multi-agent to single-agent tokens and dollars.
116e01b63a: Small breadth is a loss. At N = 1 the orchestrator uses 3.5 times the tokens and 2.35 times the cost for the same answer. The lead plans and synthesises, and the subagent pays a cold start. At N = 3 it is still 1.8 times the cost. That is why every enterprise rule of thumb includes a floor below which the lead does the work itself, and why example 05 puts that floor in code.
6ce75936c8: The crossover depends on exploration depth, not on N alone. With five turns per subagent, the designs cross near N = 10 on cost. With three turns they cross at N = 4; with eight, near N = 24; with twelve, near N = 50. A prompt that lets subagents wander for twelve turns turns a good design into a bad one. So the turn budget in the task contract (section 10) is a cost control, not a safety nicety.
81352a20c9: Caching moves the crossover. Every subagent starts with the same tool definitions and system prompt. Suppose the stable prefix is cached and billed at a fraction of the base input price; the text of the model assumes about 10 percent for cache reads (check the docs for current prices, minimum prefix sizes and cache lifetimes). Then the five-turn crossover drops from N = 10 to N = 5. Design the subagents so the prefix really is identical (chapter 5).
5b3adb2b2a: The quality limit is a different axis. At N = 30 the single agent's peak context is about 99,000 tokens, against 18,500 for the lead. Cost alone says "multi-agent wins above N = 10". Quality may say "above N = 10 the single agent is also less accurate". That has to be measured, because the cost model cannot see it.
37c6584edb:
The model is optimistic for the orchestrator in two ways. It assumes subagents succeed on the first try and need no retry. And it ignores the lead's re-planning when a subagent returns something unexpected. Retries and re-planning rounds add tokens in proportion to the failure rate. So a design whose subagents fail 10 percent of the time costs about 10 percent more, before you count the rework.

It is pessimistic for the orchestrator in one way that matters. If the single agent can fetch all 20 sites' data as parallel tool calls in a single turn, its history grows once instead of twenty times, and the quadratic term mostly disappears. That is the case the "workflow with a parallel step" option covers. It is why the ladder in section 07 asks whether each branch needs its own agentic loop before it recommends subagents.
b251da460f:
The reported industry figures belong in the same frame. Anthropic's write-up on its Research system reported roughly 4 times the tokens for a single agent against chat, and roughly 15 times for multi-agent (check the source). It argued that the extra spend paid for itself on high-value research.

Both halves of that matter for the exam. The multiplier is large, and the justification was value per task. A design that multiplies cost by 15 for a task worth cents is a wrong answer, however clever the topology. The test is mechanical:
25f00be568:
The usual cost lever in a multi-agent design is the tier split. A stronger model plans and synthesises, the two calls where judgement matters. A cheaper model runs the narrow subagent loops. Anthropic's write-up used a larger-model lead with smaller-model subagents. Chapter 4 covers how to choose per component. The architect-level rule is to run the ablation per class (section 17), because the cheaper tier lowers accuracy on some classes and not others.

The NOC's budget is $8 per incident, at about 600 incidents a month, so the monthly ceiling is $4,800. With the example's placeholder prices, a 20-site incident costs about $4.43 at five exploration turns without caching, and about $2.97 with a cached prefix. That is comfortably inside the cap. At eight exploration turns the same incident costs about $6.50 with caching. That is inside $8 but leaves little room for retries.

Example 16 shows how the budget is allocated to subagents, and what happens at 30 or 60 sites. Some subagents move to the cheaper tier, and past a point the plan is refused and escalated. Budgets are code, never prompt text.
bf4740748e: The single agent's latency is a sum over sequential work. The orchestrator's latency has three parts: the lead's planning time, the time for the subagents to finish, and the lead's synthesis time. If all N subagents could run at once, the middle term would be the maximum of N individual latencies. Three effects turn that clean statement into a design problem.
5493ab117d: Concurrency is capped. You rarely get N workers. Three things cap parallelism: your account's rate limits (requests and tokens per minute; check your own limits in the console), the downstream APIs the tools call (the performance-management system may allow eight concurrent queries), and your own thread pool. With N units and cap C, work runs in about ceil(N/C) waves. The wall-clock is roughly waves times the typical subagent latency. A pool that starts the next subagent as soon as one finishes does slightly better than strict waves, and example 02 models that.
faa1cea02b:
The maximum of noisy durations has a heavy tail. Subagent latency is not constant. Some sites have long histories, some tool calls are slow, some models decide to explore longer. If each subagent has a probability q of exceeding some threshold, the probability that at least one of N does is 1 - (1 - q)^N. With q = 5 percent and N = 20, that is 64 percent. With N = 30 it is 78 percent.

So a design can meet the SLA at the median while the slowest of thirty subagents routinely does not. That design will miss its p95. This is the arithmetic of "The Tail at Scale", and the remedies are the same. Cap per-task time, hedge the critical few, and decide in advance what the system does with a straggler.
31ec0e14b3: Rate limits are a hidden synchronisation point. Twenty subagents that each send 16,000 input tokens in the same minute make 320,000 input tokens per minute plus output. That comes on top of everything else your organisation runs. If it exceeds your limit, calls are rejected with a rate-limit error and the SDK retries with back-off, which stretches the tail further. Size concurrency against measured token throughput, not against the number of subagents. And treat a 429 as a signal to lower the cap, not a transient to hammer through.
2bccae089a:
Look at the last block of the output. It is the design decision in numeric form. Without a timeout, the 30-site p95 is 384 seconds with 100 percent coverage. A 120-second timeout cuts p95 to 313 seconds and loses about 2 percent of coverage. At 90 seconds, p95 is 285 seconds with 93 percent coverage; at 70 seconds, it is 264 seconds with 85 percent coverage.

A timeout is a purchase: it buys tail latency with completeness. Whether the purchase is acceptable is a requirements question, and the per-segment thresholds answer it. For the NOC: is a 93 percent coverage report that names the missing sites acceptable to the on-call engineer? In most designs yes, provided the report states the gaps and a coverage floor routes low-coverage reports to a human.
163e137ac6: Two further levers exist. Hedging means launching a duplicate of a slow task. It is cheap for a database read and expensive for a model run that costs tens of thousands of tokens, so use it only for the few critical-path subagents. Splitting stragglers means cutting large shards into smaller ones, which reduces variance; the decomposition section returns to this. Neither is free, and neither substitutes for a measured p95 under load.
294203e52e: Chapter 2 introduced the escalation ladder: augmented LLM, then workflow, then agent. Multi-agent is the top rung, and the discipline is to climb only as far as the requirements card forces you. The tests are ordered so that the cheapest design that satisfies the card wins. Each test is something you can check with a number or a yes/no from the card.
7bf30820ab: Example 03 encodes the ladder and applies it to eight requirements cards. The rules are deliberately simple, so that you can argue with each threshold. The shape of the reasoning is what the exam tests.
d73ff85d98:
Four of those lines deserve a sentence each.

  • The bank balance bot is a workflow. The path is known, volume is two million a day and the SLA is two seconds. Even a single agent loop is the wrong shape, and a hierarchy "for scalability" is a plain error.
  • The supplier e-mail to purchase order case is split even though its breadth is one, because the decisive property is a trust boundary.
  • The tightly coupled Spring refactor stays single because its units need each other's details. Parallel subagents editing from separate partial views would make conflicting changes.
  • The nightly store-ops digest for 600 stores is the quiet one. The path is known (a workflow, one summarising call per store), and the value per store is ten cents. An agent per store would multiply the bill past the value.

High breadth is not enough. The card must also show a branch that needs its own decisions.
a5cc616670: Suppose the 20 site look-ups are independent and cheap. Then one agent can issue them as parallel tool calls in a single turn (CCAR-F chapter 1, section 6) and reason over the results. That is the single-agent design with flat history growth, and it beats the orchestrator on cost and often on latency. Subagents earn their overhead when each branch needs several dependent steps of its own, not when each needs one fetch.
f57d474d04: A topology fixes who talks to whom, who owns the plan, who owns termination, and where state lives. CCAR-F chapter 2 teaches the hub-and-spoke mechanics. Here the question is different: given a requirements card, which topology's failure behaviour can you live with? Four shapes cover nearly everything. Two further patterns, routing and handoff, appear often enough to name.
c13a92656e:
One lead plans, delegates, collects, validates and synthesises. The lead owns the budget, the trace id, the coverage figure and the final answer. Subagents never talk to each other. If one needs another's output, the information passes through the lead, which means you can see it, log it and filter it.

Failure behaviour is the friendliest of the four. A failed subagent is a missing row in a table that the lead knows about.

There are two weaknesses. The lead's context and judgement are the bottleneck, since its context grows by the size of each summary. And the lead is a single point of failure, which the persisted plan (section 15) mitigates. This is the default answer for open-ended breadth: investigations, research, audits.
fe2129c0bf:
Fixed stages in a fixed order, each stage possibly an agent: intake, analysis, review. The order is in code, so termination, cost and audit are as predictable as a workflow. (This is the "workflow of agents" case.)

The characteristic failure is error propagation. A mistake at stage one is faithfully processed by stages two and three. The remedy is a gate between stages: code that checks that a stage's output is well-formed and consistent with known facts before the next stage spends tokens on it.

Example 17 shows the difference. The same bad ticket (sites that belong to New Jersey stamped as New York) runs through all three stages. With no gates, the reviewer approves it. With a gate, the run stops after intake and costs one stage instead of three.
2b137143ce: Notice what the review stage actually checked: that the report was internally consistent. A reviewer that sees only the analyst's report cannot detect an upstream error, because the report is consistent with the wrong premise. A review stage is worth its tokens only if it has independent evidence: its own look at the source data, a different model, or a rule check against ground truth. Otherwise it rubber-stamps.
de4ba6565e:
Leads of leads. The case for it is real but narrow: a task so broad that one lead cannot hold N summaries (hundreds of stores, thousands of contracts), where regional leads can each coordinate a subset.

The cost is information loss at every summarisation hop, quantified in section 11. If each hop keeps 70 percent of the facts that matter, three hops deliver a decisive low-salience fact less than one time in seven.

The fix is usually not a hierarchy but code-side sharding. A deterministic program partitions 600 stores into 20 shards of 30 and runs 20 flat subagents. A second, deterministic merge step (a table join, not a model) combines their structured outputs. You get the breadth without the telephone game. Reach for a true hierarchy only when sub-areas need their own planning, and cap the depth at two levels.
1851f39c0e:
Agents that read and write a shared blackboard, or message each other. It is the most flexible shape, and the one with no owner. Example 15 shows the characteristic failure. Two peers each defer to the other, and they spend 24 turns and about 18,700 tokens without reaching a conclusion, because nobody is accountable for ending. The hub-and-spoke fix costs two specialist calls and about 700 tokens, and it ends with an owner and evidence.

In a regulated setting the deeper problem is audit. With no single decision log, you cannot answer "why did the system do that" in the form a regulator or an incident review needs.
69cbe1beab:
Two patterns are easy to confuse with multi-agent designs.

A router classifies the request and sends it to one of several specialist agents. Only one specialist runs per request, so cost is roughly a single agent's plus a small classification call (chapter 2). Its failure mode is misrouting, so evaluate the router's confusion matrix per class.

A handoff transfers control from one agent to another in sequence, with the conversation state. For example, a triage agent hands a customer to a billing agent and then to a retention agent. One agent is active at a time, there is one thread, and the customer sees continuity. The hard parts are what state transfers and who may call back.

Neither gives you parallelism or context isolation, so neither belongs in the cost model above. Both are common correct answers when a scenario's real need is specialisation rather than breadth.
8cdf276a55:
A decomposition is a cut through the problem. A good cut has little information flowing across it. Each piece can be done with what it is given, and the pieces recombine with a cheap merge. A bad cut forces subagents to need what another subagent holds. That produces duplicated work, holes, conflicting decisions, and chatter.

The same principle sits behind bounded contexts in domain-driven design: cut where the interface is narrow. In practice, you evaluate each candidate cut by asking "what does piece A need to know about piece B's work?" Then you choose the axis for which the answer is "almost nothing".
c1b5c42fc3:
A retailer's procurement team wants every supplier contract checked for six topics: liability caps, data-protection terms, payment terms, termination rights, price-adjustment clauses and exclusivity. There are 40 contracts of about 25 pages, roughly 14,000 tokens each, or 560,000 tokens in total. Evaluate two cuts.

By topic gives six subagents, and each must read all 40 contracts. That is 560,000 tokens per context. It exceeds the context window of the models in this guide (check current limits in the docs), and it wastes five-sixths of every read.

By contract gives 40 subagents. Each reads 14,000 tokens and extracts all six topics into a fixed schema. That means contexts of about 20,000 tokens, linear cost, and a clean merge. Cross-contract questions ("which contracts have a liability cap below the policy minimum") are then answered by the lead, or better by a deterministic query, over 40 structured records.

The entity cut wins because information flows within a contract (all six topics need the same pages), not across contracts. The aspect cut would have split exactly where the information is most shared.
d037e03deb: There is a second-order decision inside each subagent. Six topics from one contract can be extracted in one call with one schema. Splitting them into six aspect subagents per contract would re-read the same 14,000 tokens six times for no gain, unless a topic needs long, separate reasoning (a complex indemnification analysis). That is the over-decomposition error: applying a second axis where the first already produced pieces of the right size.
74b99a044b:
Fixed overhead per subagent (cold start in time and tokens) pushes towards bigger shards. Parallelism and tail control push towards smaller ones. The trade has an answer you can compute.

Take 600 stores and a nightly exception review. There are 20 concurrent workers, a 15-second and 6,400-token cold start per subagent, and 4 seconds and 1,800 tokens of work per store. Example 11 sweeps the shard size.
e44a89f01d:
One store per subagent needs 30 waves and 570 seconds, and burns 4.9 million tokens, most of it on cold starts. Sixty stores per subagent leaves only 10 subagents on 20 workers. Half the capacity is idle, and wall-clock climbs to 255 seconds. The best wall-clock is at 30 stores per shard: 20 subagents, exactly one wave, 135 seconds, and a token bill (1.2 million) close to the large-shard minimum.

The rule that falls out is to make the number of shards about equal to the concurrency cap, with equal sizes. Shrink shards further only when a single shard's context gets too large, or its latency variance threatens the SLA. Balance the shards by estimated work (token size), not by item count, or a few huge items make stragglers.
933adf0b5a: When the items are enumerable, never let the lead model decide which items belong to which subagent. A model-written plan overlaps and leaves holes, the same way an engineer asked to split a list "roughly in half" in prose does. Example 11 checks a prose plan against the universe of sites, and a code plan against the same check. The model's plan misses a site, assigns two sites to two subagents, and invents a site that does not exist.
240d568000:
The same check runs again after the subagents return, against what actually came back. Every item in scope is either present with a valid result or named in the not-analysed list. A coverage identity (analysed + failed = in scope, and nothing outside scope) is the cheapest correctness test in a multi-agent system. It catches the worst class of silent failure.

Sometimes the cut genuinely requires judgement, as in an aspect decomposition of an unstructured question. Then let the model propose the pieces, and have code check that the proposed scopes are disjoint and exhaustive against a stated checklist. Reject the plan if they are not.
09b684e154:
When a Spring team builds two services that talk, they write an API contract and a consumer-driven test, because the cost of ambiguity is paid in production. The lead-to-subagent boundary deserves the same. The lead sends a natural-language brief, and the subagent sends back JSON. The contract is the structured form of both directions: what the subagent is asked, what it may use, what it may spend, and what shape and quality of answer the lead will accept.

CCAR-F chapter 2 (section 8) covers what makes a brief effective for the model: complete prior findings, goals and quality criteria rather than procedures, and structured results that separate content from metadata. This section covers the other half: the mechanical checks that let the lead reject a bad return without reading it.
bcebb5cf9c:
Each field exists because its absence caused a failure somewhere.

  • scope and out_of_scope prevent duplicated and missing work.
  • tools enforces least privilege per subagent, not per system.
  • output_schema makes the return machine-checkable.
  • The three budgets (budget_turns, budget_tokens, timeout_s) are the circuit breakers from CCAR-F chapter 1. They are sized well above normal runs, and they raise when exceeded.
  • meta carries the trace id and any identifiers the tools need.

Two details are easy to miss. First, the contract must permit an honest failure. The return instruction says "insufficient evidence rather than guessing", and the validator accepts that value. Otherwise the schema forces the model to fabricate. Second, the schema requires evidence ids for every claim, so the lead and a human reviewer can follow any statement back to a record.
2030b05a5f:
The validator is small on purpose. It checks shape (JSON, required keys), range (confidence between 0 and 1) and the one semantic rule that matters most: a claim needs evidence. It does not check truth, because code cannot.

Truth is checked three ways elsewhere: a verifier subagent or rule for high-impact claims (section 14), spot checks against ground truth in evaluation (section 17), and human review for the cases that matter (chapter 13).

Treat the model's self-reported confidence as weak evidence. It is poorly calibrated unless you have calibrated it against labelled outcomes (CCAR-F chapter 16). So it can route work for review, but it cannot be the only gate.
8034b7915e:
The Java record shows the second discipline: invariants enforced where the contract is constructed. A contract with an empty scope, a 40-turn budget or a 30-minute timeout should not be constructible, whatever the lead model proposed. In a design where the lead writes contracts, the lead proposes parameters and your code builds the contract through this constructor. The model never writes a field that bypasses the checks.

Version the output schema the way you version an API. A change to probable_cause values breaks the lead's synthesis prompt, the dashboards that count causes, and every recorded evaluation.
319392d8a5: Isolation is the point of a subagent, and also its main hazard. The subagent sees exactly what you put in its brief. The lead sees exactly what the subagent returns. Anything not carried across the boundary is lost. Two design questions follow: how much to send back, and in what form.
b5c13ebd20:
Take a subagent that pulls 300 alarms, KPIs and change records. It should write the raw evidence to an artifact store (object storage, a table keyed by trace id and task id) and return a short structured summary plus a reference. The lead then holds a table of conclusions, and can fetch any underlying record on demand.

Example 07 measures three designs for the 20 degraded sites in the NOC data: handing the lead all transcripts, handing it summaries only, and handing it summaries with references.
3a4a6d76d4:
The first design costs the lead 29,338 tokens of context, nearly all of it noise. It invites exactly the quality problems isolation was meant to avoid. The second is tiny (628 tokens), but the lead cannot verify anything: a wrong conclusion looks the same as a right one. The third costs 898 tokens, which is 3 percent of the first. Fetching one artifact to check a surprising claim adds only about 1,500 more.

This is the pattern: summaries to reason over, references to verify.

Treat the artifact store as the system of record. Write each artifact once, immutably, under the trace id, with the same data classification and retention as the source data (chapter 14). An alarm history containing customer identifiers does not become unregulated by being copied into an object bucket.
0b29408e3d:
Every summary is a lossy compression, and the loss compounds across hops. The risk is not that the model forgets the loud facts. It is that the decisive fact is the unremarkable one: the maintenance window that explains the alarms, the single config push that preceded the degradation, the clause on page 22 that overrides the cap on page 4.

Example 08 models this simply. Each report has ten facts with random salience. A summariser keeps the top fraction by salience. The decisive fact has low-to-middling salience. The numbers below are the probability that it reaches the top agent.
25972f2c7a:
Three design rules follow.

  • Keep the hierarchy flat: one summarisation hop (subagent to lead) instead of three.
  • Pin what must survive: evidence ids, artifact references, and the identifiers of affected customers or sites are copied verbatim into fixed fields, never paraphrased in prose.
  • Let the lead pull detail: give it a fetch_artifact tool, so a surprising summary can be checked rather than believed.

A fourth rule applies in the other direction, from lead to subagent. If earlier findings matter for a subagent's task, include them in full in the brief (CCAR-F chapter 2). A subagent that is not told that the transport link was already ruled out will spend four turns rediscovering it.
d220e2c4a0:
In an enterprise, the strongest reason to split an agent is often not breadth. It is that one task mixes content you cannot trust with actions you cannot undo.

Prompt injection is the threat: instructions hidden in data the model reads, which the model may treat as if the operator had written them. The data might be a supplier's e-mail, a customer's chat message, a web page, or a document in a retrieval index. No prompt reliably prevents this, so the defence is architectural: an agent that reads untrusted content should not hold the tools that can do damage, and the content should reach the privileged agent only as validated, typed data.

Simon Willison's "dual LLM" pattern and his "lethal trifecta" framing express the same rule. The trifecta is private data, untrusted content and an exfiltration or action channel in one agent. Check his posts for the details. Chapter 13 covers guardrails more broadly, and chapter 7 the authorisation of tool calls. This section is the decomposition view.
66fbae6deb: Example 09 builds both designs against the same e-mail. It contains an invoice reference and an injected line telling the assistant to create a PO for $48,000 payable to an unknown account. In design A, one agent reads the mail and holds the PO tool, and the scripted model follows the injection. In design B, the reader returns typed fields, the validator applies an allow-list, and the actor receives only the clean fields.
1870275fe4:
Three details carry the design.

First, the validator uses an allow-list of keys. The free-text notes field is the only place an injection can survive, so it is dropped rather than inspected. Defences that try to detect injection in the text are a losing arms race. Defences that remove the channel are not.

Second, the validator checks fields against the system of record: the supplier is on the known list, and the reference matches the format of a real PO. A well-formed lie is still a lie.

Third, the final test is an assertion on the actor's request log. The raw e-mail text never appears in anything the actor received. That is a test you can put in CI.
3017e5b1be:
The split reduces the blast radius. It does not eliminate risk. An injection can still manipulate the values inside permitted fields (an amount of 4,800 instead of 480). That is why the approval threshold sits outside both agents, and why the actor's own tools enforce limits: a tool that refuses a payment above the caller's authority regardless of the prompt.

Notice also that the actor need not be an agent. If the next step is "match this invoice to the PO and queue payment", it is a workflow. The simplest architecture is one reader agent, one validator and a deterministic procedure.
e91151ec3f:
A carrier's care assistant reads whatever the customer types, and it may be asked to change the account: add a line, reset a voicemail PIN, request a port-out, swap a SIM. Customer text is untrusted by definition, and SIM swap and port-out are the high-value fraud targets.

The split is the same. The conversational agent reads the chat. It has read-only account tools plus one write tool, submit_change_request, which creates a typed request (type, line, requested-by). It cannot execute anything. A code path verifies the customer for that request type (a one-time code, a PIN, a step-up check). It then routes the request to a workflow that performs the change, with a human approval for the classes that policy requires.

The model's job is to understand the customer and prepare the request. The authority to execute lives elsewhere. Customer proprietary network information (CPNI) rules and your own privacy policy decide which of those steps need what authentication, and legal owns that decision (chapter 14).
454de5971c: The code filters out healthy sites before any model runs; 10 of the 30 sites in the example have no major alarm and normal drop rates. It applies a floor under which the lead does the work itself, and a ceiling on fan-out. Everything that governs cost and shape is decided here, deterministically, and logged.
2ef118aa90: Each subagent runs the stop_reason loop from CCAR-F chapter 1, with a narrower tool list, per-task accounting in a ledger, and budgets that raise. The fan-out runs contracts through a bounded pool and validates every return. It keeps going when individual tasks fail. It measures each timeout from the moment the task starts, not from submission; otherwise queue time would count as slowness.
170126c378: One property of this code deserves a remark. A Python thread cannot be killed, so a timed-out subagent is abandoned and its late result is discarded. In production, subagent calls go through an HTTP client with its own request timeout and a cancellation token (or, in Java, an interruptible call on a virtual thread). That way an abandoned task actually stops spending tokens. Check how your client library handles cancellation, and set both layers.
4ab77da2d8:
The run produces a 100 percent coverage report, with 20 of 20 conclusions matching the synthetic ground truth, for about $0.23 at the placeholder prices. The lead's synthesis call consumed about 1,300 tokens, while the subagents consumed about 62,000.

The most useful line is the assessment: ten of the twenty degraded sites report the same transport signature. The subagents could not see that, because each looked at one site. Only the lead sees the pattern. So it needs one more tool that the subagents lack: the transport topology, so it can check whether those ten sites share a backhaul path. And the output should open with one transport ticket rather than ten. That correlation step is the lead's real job, and the reason it sits on the stronger model tier.
37da03f7f3:
For a Java/Spring estate, the orchestrator is an ordinary service.

  • The plan and status live in a table: a SubtaskRun entity, written before the subagent runs.
  • A semaphore is the concurrency cap, not the thread-pool size. With virtual threads on Java 21 you can have thousands of threads; the limit you care about is the rate limit and the downstream quota.
  • The status enum carries the distinction between timeout, budget exhaustion and contract violation that retry logic needs.
65b44d1b20: The service resumes by skipping rows already DONE, which is what makes a restart safe (section 15). It throws when the plan exceeds the cap, instead of silently trimming it, because a silently truncated plan is a coverage hole nobody reported. And the coverage floor produces a human-routed report, not a customer-facing one.
77d1d79042: A single agent has one way to fail completely. A fan-out of N subagents has N ways to fail partially. That is worse in one respect and better in another. It is worse because partial results are easy to present as complete. It is better because you can design for it, as you would for a scatter-gather query over shards.
f3a7f4edf6: If each subagent independently returns a valid result with probability p, the probability that all N do is p^N. At p = 0.99 and N = 20 that is 82 percent. At p = 0.95 it is 36 percent, and at p = 0.90 it is 12 percent. A pipeline that requires all N is therefore unusable at realistic reliabilities. The design requirement is not "every subagent succeeds". It is "the system produces a correct, honest report when some do not".
00097a7acd: Example 06 injects three faults into a ten-site fan-out. One site's alarm API hangs (a timeout). One subagent returns a conclusion with no evidence (a contract violation). And one is limited to a single model turn (a budget breach). The example then applies the retry policy.
ad24de8af5:
The first pass delivers 7 of 10. The retry policy re-runs only the failures that can change: the timeout (the retry uses a healthy API) and the contract violation (the second attempt answers correctly). The budget breach is not retried with the same budget, because it would fail the same way. It is either widened deliberately or left in the not-analysed list.

After one retry, coverage is 90 percent, exactly at the floor in the example. So the report goes out with site-NYC-04510 named as not analysed. One point lower, and the report would route to a human queue instead.

That is the shape of a good partial-failure design: bounded retries, honest gaps, a floor, and a routing decision.
0b17028b88:
The p^N arithmetic assumes independence, and the worst failures break it. When the performance-management API is down, all twenty subagents fail. Each burns its retries and some of its budget before giving up.

The remedy is a circuit breaker over the first wave. If more than a set fraction of the first C subagents (say 40 percent) fail for the same reason, stop launching the rest, record the reason, and escalate to a human or retry later. This bounds the damage to one wave of failed work instead of N. It turns a mysterious bill into a named outage.
9342eb3f2c:
A subagent that is wrong produces a confident, well-formed, evidence-looking answer. The lead incorporates it, and the synthesis presents it with the authority of the whole system. Two controls help.

First, the schema's evidence requirement lets you check that the cited alarm id exists and has the claimed code. That is a mechanical test of whether the claim is grounded.

Second, for claims that trigger expensive actions (dispatching a power crew, rolling back a parameter push), add an independent verifier. This is a second pass that sees the raw evidence and the claim, and answers only whether the evidence supports it. Use code where a rule can check the claim, and a different model or prompt where it cannot.

Apply verification by impact, not universally. It doubles the cost of the claims it covers, so scope it to the actions with real consequences. Size the sample from the evaluation's measured error rate (chapter 11).
ba63b4929e:
Subagents that run in parallel and write to the same resource produce the same bugs as threads that share mutable state. The rule is the same: one writer. Subagents read and propose. One component (the lead, a workflow step, or a human) applies changes, with idempotency keys and an audit entry.

For coding agents, this is the strongest argument for keeping tightly coupled edits in one thread. It is also why worktree isolation, or branch-per-agent plus a merge step, is used when parallel code changes are unavoidable (chapter 17 for team practice).
dc23fd053d: In a single agent, the state is the transcript. In a multi-agent system, state is spread across a plan, N subtask statuses, N artifacts and the lead's context. Say the orchestrator process dies after 5 of 12 subtasks. Do you re-run all twelve, wasting tokens and repeating side effects, or resume the seven that remain? The design answer is the same as for any long-running job.
2c3681a207: Persist the plan before running it. A table with one row per subtask (contract, status, attempts, result reference, tokens, tier, trace id) is the orchestrator's memory. A restart or a compaction can wipe the lead's context without losing the plan. Anthropic's write-up of its Research system described saving the plan to memory for this reason (check the source).
7c271e3bb6: Resume by status. On restart, skip DONE rows, re-run PLANNED and RUNNING rows, and report FAILED and TIMED_OUT rows. A RUNNING row is ambiguous: did the side effect happen before the crash? So every side-effecting tool must be safe to repeat.
e3a5698d53:
The output shows both halves. After a crash with 5 rows DONE, the resume run executes exactly 7 subtasks and ends with 12 tickets, not 17.

The last two lines show why the key matters. Re-running RUNNING rows through the idempotent tool leaves the ticket count unchanged. The non-idempotent tool creates three duplicates from three repeats. In a telecom setting a duplicate ticket is an annoyance. A duplicate credit or a duplicate service order is an incident.

A durable workflow engine gives you retries, timers and history out of the box, with the model calls as activities. Temporal and AWS Step Functions are examples of the category; check what your platform standardises on. Whether you build the table yourself or adopt an engine, the properties above are the requirement.
cb7f24c108: CCAR-P rewards the answer where governance is part of the architecture. It punishes the answer where governance is bolted on after the pilot. A multi-agent system multiplies the surfaces governance has to cover: more identities, more tool grants, more places where regulated data lands, more logs to join. The design rule is to give each control one home that does not depend on what any model decides.
b791aef5d4:
Three points tie the table to this chapter's design choices.

First, read-only subagents are a governance decision as much as a safety one. With a read-only tool list, most subagent failures are wasted tokens, not incidents. It also makes the approval boundary obvious, because changes happen in one place.

Second, the budget is a control, not a metric. Example 16 allocates an incident ceiling across subagents. It downgrades the tier when the projection exceeds the ceiling, and it refuses plans that cannot fit even on the cheaper tier.
3c3c293288:
At 30 sites the ceiling forces 24 subagents onto the worker tier and 6 onto the cheaper one. At 60 sites only 9 can stay on the worker tier.

The breaker at the end shows the enforcement. A third charge pushes a subagent past its cap, and the run raises. The subtask is marked BUDGET_EXHAUSTED with its partial evidence preserved, and the lead reports it in the not-analysed list.

Third, the kill switch must exist before the incident. A flag that disables fan-out and routes incidents to the single-agent path or to a human queue is cheap to build. It is very expensive to improvise at 3 a.m. when a downstream outage is burning budget.
b78aeb88ff:
Chapter 11 covers evaluation metrics and datasets in general. Multi-agent systems add four problems:

  • the path varies from run to run, so exact-step comparisons are meaningless;
  • there are two kinds of component (lead and subagents) and one end result;
  • the claim you are testing is comparative: is this better than the simpler design?
  • there are per-segment thresholds, and they are literal.

Evaluate at four levels.
d3fdf77f20: End to end on outcomes. Run complete incidents or audits and score the final answer against labels, per segment. Repeat at least three times to estimate run-to-run variance. Grade outcomes (was the root cause right, with valid evidence?), not step sequences.
a444a716a1:
Say the requirement is "85 percent correct per incident class". Then the aggregate does not matter. Every class must clear its own bar, and the bar must be demonstrated, not merely observed in a small sample. With a sample of 30 and an observed 93 percent, a 95 percent Wilson interval still reaches down to 0.79, so you cannot claim 85 percent.

Example 14 builds the harness on synthetic fixtures and applies the gate to the lower bound. The fixtures are not measurements; replace them with your runs.
a074c847af:
Read the table in three passes.

Gate by class. The orchestrator clears transport, RAN-config and interference. Neither design clears power, but only because 30 cases are too few. The corrective is more labelled cases (at n = 60 and 95 percent observed, the lower bound is 0.86), not a different architecture.

Paired comparison. Both designs ran the same cases, so the right test counts disagreements: 27 cases only the orchestrator got right, and 2 only the single agent got right. McNemar's statistic is 19.9 (significant at the 5 percent level), so the improvement is not noise.

Cost per correct answer: $2.36 against $3.51. The orchestrator is more expensive per correct answer overall. But the decision lives in the marginal view by class. It costs about $7 to $9 per additional correct answer on transport, RAN-config and interference incidents. On power incidents, where the single agent was already at 93 percent, it costs about $45 per additional correct answer.

That last number is the argument for a hybrid. An incident whose first look says "mains failure at one site" does not need a fan-out, and that is what the scaling rule's floor and filters already do.
4b342ab081:
The median incident costs $0.055 at the placeholder prices, and the p95 is $0.10. But one incident costs $0.33, 5.9 times the median. The over-spawn alert explains why: its planner launched 30 subagents, including healthy sites, because the code-side filter was missing in that path.

The drill-down by subtask shows the cost is spread evenly (about 1 cent each). That says "too many subagents", not "one runaway subagent". Those are two different fixes, and you can tell them apart only because every call is attributed to a trace and a task.

Set alerts on these signals:

  • cost per trace against the median (not against a fixed number that drifts with prices);
  • subagents per trace against the cap;
  • coverage below the floor;
  • contract-violation rate per subagent type;
  • the share of runs that hit a budget breaker.

Chapter 10 covers the observability stack, and chapter 12 the A/B testing and cost optimisation that act on these signals.
2af42e9613: A lead asked to "decompose and delegate" will sometimes decompose by site and by aspect, producing three subagents per site. The code below launches whatever the lead proposes. The fix moves the decision about how many subagents, and on which axis, into code. It then checks the proposal against that decision rather than trusting it.
8c3d6ce794:
For a regional query over 30 sites, the broken path launches 90 subagents (about $5.00 at the placeholder prices). The fixed path filters to the 20 active sites. It notices that one subagent per site (entity axis) exceeds the cap of 8, and refuses with a message that says what to do: batch into waves or narrow the scope.

The refusal is the important part. The wrong fix is to silently keep the first 8 sites, which converts an expensive error into a quiet coverage hole.
d6a554ae67: Single-agent baseline. Example 02 models sequential work. For 30 sites the median is 971 seconds and p95 1,104 seconds, so the single agent fails the SLA before quality is considered. Its peak context (about 99,000 tokens in example 01) also puts accuracy at risk. Measured on historical incidents (in the example's fixtures), transport accuracy is 73 percent, below the gate. Both binding numbers are failed, so the ladder allows a fan-out.
2fb1a4d0e2: Latency. The performance-management API quota caps concurrency at 8, so 20 subagents run in three waves. In example 02 that gives p50 about 293 seconds and p95 about 380 seconds for 30 sites. A 120-second per-task timeout brings p95 to 313 seconds at about 98 percent coverage. Both meet 900 seconds, with room for the lead's planning and synthesis.
36b03fa88f: Cost. At five exploration turns per subagent, a 20-site incident costs about $4.43 uncached and $2.97 with the stable prefix cached (example 01, placeholder prices). That is inside the $8 cap, and roughly $1,800 a month at 600 incidents if all incidents are 20-site. Eight exploration turns would put it at $6.50 cached, too close to the cap once retries are counted. So the contract caps exploration at 6 turns, and the ledger enforces it.
602fcf8721: Failure design. Retry timeouts and contract violations once. Never retry budget breaches. Set the first-wave breaker at 40 percent failures. A coverage floor of 90 percent routes to a human queue. The report always lists not-analysed sites.
7e875fef2f: Proof and decision record. Run shadow mode on the previous quarter's incidents, with at least 60 labelled cases per class, so the lower bound can be shown to clear 85 percent. The architecture decision record lists the single-agent baseline numbers as the rejected alternative. It sets review triggers (cost per incident above $6, any class below its gate, coverage below 90 percent in more than 5 percent of incidents) and names the owner.
a23d67f85e: Which binding number is there? Latency is not binding (overnight). Quality is (95 percent per type). Cost matters, since this is a quarterly audit and legal is expensive. Context is binding for the aspect cut (560,000 tokens across 40 contracts), but not for the entity cut (about 14,000 per contract).
30d4b169df: Do we need agents at all? The path is known: read one contract, extract six fields with citations. That is a workflow with one structured-output call per contract. The schedule is overnight, so each call can use the Batch API (50 percent cheaper, completes within 24 hours; check the docs for current terms and limits). The Batch API supports single-turn requests but not multi-turn tool use. Forty independent single-turn extractions, run as a batch, then a deterministic merge into the table: that is the simplest architecture that works, and it is not multi-agent.
c3fb0dbee3: Where do agents earn their place? Some contracts reference exhibits, amendments or master agreements outside the 14,000 tokens, and those need a loop that fetches them. A cross-reference detector, or an extraction that returns "see Exhibit C", identifies them. Route those to a subagent with a document-fetch tool. Expect a minority. The multi-agent design handles the tail; the workflow handles the bulk.
b4ee2a610c: Quality gate per type, literal. Measure field accuracy separately for supply, logistics and licensing on a labelled set. Say licensing is at 91 percent while the overall is 96 percent. The launch is blocked until the licensing prompt or schema is fixed, because the requirement is per type. With 95 percent as the threshold, size the labelled set so the lower bound of the interval can be shown to clear it. That means more than 60 fields per type; tens of contracts per type is more realistic.
4f7d241090: Governance. Contracts are confidential. Process them under the vendor agreement and data terms legal has approved (chapter 14). Do not copy contract text into logs. Retain artifacts under the contract-record retention policy. Store citations so a lawyer can verify any value in under a minute.
b4cd172040: The second scenario teaches the discipline the chapter has been building towards. A strong CCAR-P answer is willing to say three things: the multi-agent design is for the exceptional tail of the workload, the bulk is a workflow, and the cheapest architecture satisfying the card wins.
060bc0b172: The deciding facts are a known path, one lookup, high volume and a 2-second p95. The ladder ends at "workflow or single call". A coordinator adds at least two model calls, and their variance, to every query. At two million queries a day, that multiplies the cost of a coordinator that adds no value. A and B are the "sounds scalable" distractors: scale comes from stateless horizontal replicas of a cheap path, not from agents. D changes the model but not the problem, and a larger model would slow the response further.
0380a99fab: Duplicates and holes are symptoms of a partition written in prose with vague scopes. C addresses both causes. It gives a deterministic, exhaustive, disjoint partition, and a coverage identity that catches any residual gap. A improves the proposal but cannot guarantee disjointness. B increases duplication. D is the peer anti-pattern: it adds chatter and tokens with no owner of the outcome.
42b9cc1d14: The deciding fact is that untrusted text and an irreversible tool share one agent. A is probabilistic, and the model may weigh it against the injected text. B is a pattern-matching arms race that attackers vary around. D adds friction to every legitimate PO, and it still shows the privileged agent the attack text. C removes the channel. The injected text can survive only in a field the validator drops, and the PO tool is never reachable from the component that reads the mail. Thresholds and tool-side limits remain as defence in depth.
3af4c99b52: The simpler design meets every binding number, and the difference in accuracy is within noise. The rule is the simplest architecture that satisfies the card. A treats accuracy as unbounded value, but the card sets thresholds, not maximisation. C is a preference, not a requirement. D doubles cost and adds a selection step with no evaluation behind it. The team may expect growth in breadth that would change the binding numbers. If so, the answer is to record the review trigger in the decision record, not to adopt the more complex design now.
8275ac523c: Two facts decide: the bill (600 cold starts, a lead per region) and the lost detail (summarisation at each hop). B matches the shard-size analysis. Shards roughly equal to the concurrency cap minimise wall-clock and cold-start cost. Structured outputs with references keep detail intact. And the merge is code, so there is one summarisation hop instead of three. A lowers the unit price but keeps both structural problems. C blows the lead's context. D changes the requirement without asking whether it can be met.
552fd66dd1: The failures are correlated (one dependency), so independence-based reasoning and per-task retries make it worse. Every task pays for retries against a dead service. C bounds the damage to one wave and names the cause. A makes each failed task slower and more expensive. B removes protection against transient failures in the normal case. D hands a cost-control decision to the component that cannot see the aggregate spend. Budgets and breakers belong in code.
bf533a3610:
Done when:

  • you can reproduce the cost crossover and the latency trade-off from your own measurements;
  • you have seen the trust-split assertion fail when the channel is reopened;
  • you can explain, for a workload you know, which of the six ladder tests ends the case for or against multi-agent.
